analysis.one_liner: Requires power plants in states upwind of the Adirondacks to cut acid rain pollution.
analysis.headline: A bipartisan bill to cut the sulfur dioxide and nitrogen oxide pollution causing acid rain in the Adirondacks never got a vote, dying in a House subcommittee after its 28 cosponsors from both parties did nothing more to move it.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have ordered the EPA to write rules requiring power plants in states whose emissions blow into the Adirondacks to cut sulfur dioxide deeply enough, by 2000, to restore the acidity balance of the region's lakes and streams to something close to 1984 survey levels. It would also have required major upwind plants to install modern nitrogen oxide controls. Utilities could comply with scrubbers, low-sulfur fuel, efficiency upgrades, or other proven methods, but the reductions could not be double-counted toward any other Clean Air Act obligation.
analysis.who_benefits: People who live in and visit the Adirondacks, where acid rain has killed fish and damaged hundreds of lakes and streams, would get a federally enforceable cleanup targeted at the specific upwind power plants causing the damage. Downwind communities across the Northeast would breathe less sulfur dioxide and nitrogen oxide, pollutants linked to respiratory illness and smog. Eastern forests, streams, and the region's tourism economy would also benefit.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Adirondack residents, anglers, and Northeastern downwind communities

how_it_helps.text: Requires EPA to set sulfur dioxide limits for utility units in subregions that contribute to Adirondack acid deposition, calibrated so that by 2000 the region's surface waters regain more of their acid-neutralizing capacity than measured in the 1984 National Surface Water Survey
Requires major contributing power plants to install reasonably available nitrogen oxide control technology no later than January 1, 2000
Gives utilities flexible ways to comply, including scrubbers, fuel switching, energy efficiency, burner modifications, and clean coal technologies, rather than dictating a single method
Prevents utilities from using the new reductions as credits to emit more elsewhere under the existing acid rain allowance trading program, so the cleanup would be real and additional

analysis.who_pays: Coal-burning electric utilities in the upwind subregions, chiefly in the Midwest, would bear the cost of cutting emissions, and those costs would be passed on in part to electricity customers. The bill's ban on counting these reductions toward other Clean Air Act obligations means utilities could not offset the cost by selling credits under the acid rain trading program.
analysis.who_pays_short: Midwestern coal-burning utilities and their customers

drawbacks.text: Compliance costs for upwind utilities would flow through to electricity ratepayers, and the bill forbids using the required reductions as tradeable allowances, which forecloses the cheapest flexibility the existing acid rain program offers

The bill targets a single region's problem with mandates on specific subregions rather than the economy-wide emissions trading of the 1990 Clean Air Act Amendments, a design its critics could call inefficient even though the damage it addresses was documented

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The scientific case in the bill is concrete: acid deposition had degraded Adirondack surface waters below the 1984 baseline, and the bill sets a measurable recovery target with a deadline and flexible compliance methods. The honest cost is that upwind utilities and their customers would pay for controls, and the no-double-counting rule makes that bill higher than a pure trading approach would allow. On balance the environmental and public health gain for a documented, region-specific harm outweighs a bounded utility cost, but the bill's one-region design is a fair target for cost-effectiveness criticism.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the House Commerce Committee the day it was introduced, sent to its Health and Environment Subcommittee a week later, and nothing ever happened to it; it died when the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Gerald Solomon of New York introduced the bill on November 28, 1995, and it was referred to the House Committee on Commerce
On December 5, 1995, it was referred to the Subcommittee on Health and Environment, where it stayed with no hearings, no markup, and no vote
It drew 28 cosponsors split 12 Republicans and 16 Democrats, a bipartisan roster, but no version of the bill was ever reported out of committee or brought to the floor
The 104th Congress ended on January 3, 1997, and the bill expired with it

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Coal-burning utilities in the upwind subregions and the high-sulfur coal industry gained by avoiding new emission mandates and control costs through the end of the decade. The Adirondacks and downwind Northeastern communities got nothing.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Coal-burning utilities that avoided new mandates

against.what_they_did: Would have borne the compliance costs; the chamber's inaction on the bill is consistent with the committee's historic reluctance to tighten Clean Air Act requirements on upwind coal plants

sides.party_line_note: Sponsorship was genuinely bipartisan, 12 Republicans and 16 Democrats among the 28 cosponsors, and the bill died in committee rather than on a party-line vote.

industries.industry: Coal-burning electric utilities in upwind states
industries.note: The bill would have required these plants to cut sulfur dioxide and install nitrogen oxide controls by 2000, with the costs passed on partly to ratepayers. Its death left the 1990 acid rain program's looser national caps as the only constraint.
Fuel switching to lower-sulfur coal was an explicit compliance option, so the bill would have shifted some demand away from high-sulfur coal. Its failure preserved the existing market.
The bill listed scrubber and catalytic reduction technology among compliance methods, which would have created equipment demand. With no action taken, that market never opened.
